questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Which tool helps you **observe** the tiny hairs on an ant's leg?
options: a stopwatch
a measuring jug
a forcemeter
a hand lens
questions.explanation: A hand lens makes small things look bigger so you can see more detail. The other tools measure time, volume and force.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: In a fair test you change only ___ thing and keep everything else the ___.
questions.explanation: If you change more than one thing, you cannot tell which change caused the result. A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Match each measurement to the best tool.
pairs: how hard you pull a rope
how much juice is in a glass
questions.explanation: Choose the tool made for the thing you are measuring: a thermometer for temperature, a stopwatch for time, a forcemeter for force, a jug for volume and a ruler for length.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Put the steps of an investigation in the right order.
questions.explanation: Scientists ask a question and predict first, then plan a fair test, collect and record the evidence, and only then write a conclusion.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: The class investigates: Which ball bounces highest? Sort each part of the plan.
items: the height the ball is dropped from
the floor the ball lands on
the person who reads the ruler
questions.explanation: We change only the type of ball, measure the bounce height, and keep everything else the same so the test is fair.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Which graph is best? Sort the results.
items: temperature of a cup of tea every minute
water level in a tank every hour
number of rickshaws of each colour
growth of one bean seedling each day
questions.explanation: Use a bar chart to compare separate things. Use a line graph when one thing changes over time.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: A prediction is a wild guess that does not need a reason.
questions.explanation: A prediction says what you think will happen and why. The reason comes from what you already know, for example: 'The ball will bounce higher from higher up, because it is moving faster when it lands.'

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Why do scientists repeat their measurements?
options: to make the test last longer
so they can trust results that are close together
because the first result is always wrong
so they can change something new each time
questions.explanation: If repeated results are close together, we can trust them more. The first result is not always wrong, and changing something new would make the test unfair.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Moung flew his paper plane once. It went 6 m. He says, 'Now I know how far it flies.' What advice would you give him, and why?
questions.model_answer: Fly it several times and find the mean, because one result could be a mistake or just luck. Results that are close together are more reliable.
questions.explanation: One measurement might be wrong. Repeating the test, then using the mean, makes the result more reliable.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: A globe is an example of a ___: a way of showing an idea that is too big, too small or too slow to see.
questions.explanation: Scientists use models such as globes, drawings and diagrams to explain things we cannot easily see for ourselves.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: A globe is a model of the Earth. What is one **limitation** of this model?
options: It is far smaller than the real Earth, so it cannot show every detail.
It shows where the oceans and continents are.
It lets us see the whole Earth at once.
It shows the shape of the Earth well.
questions.explanation: A model helps us understand, but it is never exactly like the real thing. A globe is tiny and cannot show real mountains, weather or cities.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Why do scientists share their results with other scientists?
questions.model_answer: So that other scientists can check the results by repeating the tests, find any mistakes, and build on the ideas to make new discoveries.
questions.explanation: Sharing lets others check the evidence, spot mistakes and use the ideas to find out more. Science grows when people share.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Class 4A investigates how the drop height changes the bounce of a ball. Put their steps in a sensible order.
sequence: Choose the heights to drop the ball from.
Drop the ball from one height and measure the bounce.
Work out the mean bounce for each height.
Draw a line graph of the means.
Describe the pattern in the graph.
Write a conclusion and say if the prediction was right.
questions.explanation: Plan first, then measure and repeat, then process the data (means and a graph), look for a pattern and finally conclude.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Look at the three thermometers. Which one shows the **highest** temperature?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 5, 25 and 40 degrees Celsius.
options: A
B
C
questions.explanation: The liquid rises higher when the temperature is higher. Thermometer C reads 40 °C, more than B (25 °C) or A (5 °C).

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: A healthy person's body temperature is about 37 °C. Which thermometer shows this?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 12, 37 and 48 degrees Celsius.
options: A
B
C
questions.explanation: Thermometer B reads 37 °C. A (12 °C) is cool and C (48 °C) is far too hot for a body.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Rafi pulls a sled with the forcemeter shown. What is the reading? Choose the answer with the right unit.
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter reading 7 newtons.
options: 7 g
7 N
7 cm
7 ml
questions.explanation: A forcemeter measures force in newtons (N). Grams measure mass, centimetres measure length and millilitres measure volume.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Match each tool to what it measures.
questions.explanation: A stopwatch measures time, a thermometer measures temperature, a ruler measures length and a balance measures mass.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: One bag of rice makes the forcemeter read as shown. Two identical bags hung together would make it read ___ N.
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter reading 4 newtons.
questions.explanation: The forcemeter reads 4 N for one bag. Two identical bags pull twice as hard: 4 + 4 = 8 N.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Tuli wants to find out which of three tea bags makes the darkest tea. She puts one in a big cup of cold water, one in a small cup of hot water and one in a mug of warm water. What should she do to make it a fair test?
options: Use a different size of cup for each tea bag.
Leave each tea bag in for as long as she likes.
Use the same amount of water at the same temperature for each tea bag.
Use cold water for the tea bag she likes best.
questions.explanation: Only the tea bag should change. The cup size, amount of water, water temperature and time must all stay the same.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: A farmer near Rajshahi wants to know how much milk his cow gives each morning. Which tool and unit should he use?
options: a ruler, in centimetres
a measuring jug, in litres
a thermometer, in °C
a forcemeter, in newtons
questions.explanation: Milk is a liquid, so we measure its volume with a measuring jug in litres (l) or millilitres (ml).

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Imran grew a bean plant on a sunny window sill. His cousin Nadia grew a different kind of plant in a bigger pot with more water, in a dark room. Imran's plant grew taller, so Imran says this proves that sunlight makes plants grow taller. Is Imran right?
questions.explanation: The plants differed in kind, pot size, water and light, so we cannot tell which change made the difference. A fair test changes only the light.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Anika wants to test which kind of cloth dries fastest on the washing line. Which things must she keep the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the size of each piece of cloth
how wet each piece is at the start
the place on the line (sun or shade)
the kind of cloth
how long each piece takes to dry
questions.explanation: The kind of cloth is what she changes, and the drying time is what she measures. Size, starting wetness and place must stay the same.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Moung timed how long an ice cube took to melt in the sun. His three trials gave 8 min, 9 min and 21 min. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore all three results.
Add the three times and use the total.
Check the 21-minute trial and repeat it.
Choose the biggest number to be safe.
questions.explanation: 21 min is very different from the other two. It may be a mistake, such as starting the timer late, so he should check it and measure again.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Scientists in Dhaka test a new vaccine on 2000 volunteers. They give the vaccine to 1000 people and no vaccine to the other 1000, then count how many in each group become ill. Why do they use two groups?
options: to compare the groups and see if the vaccine really makes a difference
to use up the spare vaccine
to make sure nobody becomes ill
to keep the groups small and easy to manage
questions.explanation: The group without the vaccine shows what happens anyway. Comparing the two groups shows whether the vaccine makes a difference.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Example class data: bean plants given 0, 25, 50 and 100 ml of water each day grew to 2, 9, 15 and 16 cm after two weeks. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: More water always makes plants grow taller, with no limit.
Water makes no difference to how tall the plants grow.
The plant given 100 ml of water was harmed by too much water.
The plants grew taller with more water, but above 50 ml there was hardly any extra growth.
questions.explanation: The height rose a lot from 0 to 50 ml, but only from 15 cm to 16 cm between 50 and 100 ml. The data do not show any harm, so that claim goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Class 4B (example data) dropped a ball three times from each height. From 100 cm the bounces were 55 cm, 61 cm and 58 cm. From 200 cm they were 110 cm, 116 cm and 113 cm. How much higher is the mean bounce from 200 cm than from 100 cm?
options: 58 cm
113 cm
55 cm
171 cm
questions.explanation: Mean from 100 cm = (55 + 61 + 58) ÷ 3 = 58 cm. Mean from 200 cm = (110 + 116 + 113) ÷ 3 = 113 cm. The difference is 113 − 58 = 55 cm.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Sami plans to find out which paper towel is strongest when wet. He will use a big piece of towel A and a small piece of towel B, pour 50 ml of water on A and 100 ml on B, hang the same mass from each, wet both in the same classroom, and test each towel three times. Which parts make his test unfair? Choose all that are right.
options: using different sizes of towel
pouring different amounts of water
hanging the same mass from each
wetting both towels in the same classroom
testing each towel three times
questions.explanation: Only the type of towel should change. Different sizes and different amounts of water are extra changes. The same mass, same room and repeats are good practice.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: In a vaccine trial (example data) 1000 children got the vaccine and 12 became ill. 1000 children did not get it and 60 became ill. Do the results support the idea that the vaccine protects children? Use the numbers in your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes. Only 12 of the 1000 children who had the vaccine became ill, compared with 60 of the 1000 who did not. That is five times more without the vaccine, so the vaccine seems to protect them.
questions.explanation: The group with the vaccine had far fewer ill children (12 compared with 60), and both groups were the same size. 60 ÷ 12 = 5, so the evidence supports the prediction.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Class 4C tested each kind of paper towel once. Towel A absorbed 18 ml of water, towel B 25 ml and towel C 31 ml. Which statement is best?
options: Towel A is the worst towel and nobody should ever use it.
All three towels absorb the same amount of water.
Towel C is the best towel in the world for every job.
Towel C absorbed the most in this test, but we should repeat the test to be sure.
questions.explanation: Each towel was tested only once, so there is not enough evidence to be sure or to say anything about every job. Repeating the test would make the results more reliable.

questions.title: Science Detectives: Working Scientifically
questions.stem: Class 4A found these mean bounces (example data): drop 50 cm gave 29 cm, 100 cm gave 58 cm, 150 cm gave 88 cm and 200 cm gave 116 cm. Use the pattern to predict the mean bounce from a drop of 250 cm: about ___ cm.
questions.explanation: Each extra 50 cm of drop height adds about 29 cm to the bounce (the bounce is a bit more than half the drop). So from 250 cm: 116 + 29 = about 145 cm.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Earthworms, moles and many ants live under the ground. What do we call these animals?
options: fossorial animals
arboreal animals
aerial animals
aquatic animals
questions.explanation: Fossorial animals live under the ground. Aerial animals fly, arboreal animals live in trees and aquatic animals live in water.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Match each animal to its vertebrate group.
questions.explanation: The five groups of vertebrates are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. A bat is a mammal even though it flies, because it has fur and feeds its babies milk.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Sort these animals into those with a backbone and those without.
questions.explanation: Vertebrates have a backbone and a skeleton inside. Spiders, crabs, earthworms and butterflies are invertebrates: they have no backbone.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Your skull ___ your brain, and muscles ___ on bones to make them move.
questions.explanation: The hard skull protects the soft brain. Muscles can only pull, never push, so they work in pairs to move a bone back and forth.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: A shark has a skeleton made of hard bone, just like a hilsa fish.
questions.explanation: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, the same bendy material as the tip of your nose. A hilsa has a skeleton of bone.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: What is an **adaptation**?
options: a journey to another place at the same time each year
the place where an animal lives
a kind of animal that has died out everywhere
a feature that helps an animal survive in its habitat
questions.explanation: An adaptation is a body feature, like webbed feet or striped fur, that helps an animal survive. Travelling each year is migration, and the home is the habitat.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Match each beak to the food it is adapted for.
pairs: long and sharp like a spear (kingfisher)
long and thin like a straw (sunbird)
questions.explanation: A beak's shape suits the food a bird eats: a spear for catching fish, a strong hook for cracking seeds, a straw for sipping nectar and a hook for tearing meat.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Put the story of a migrating duck in the right order.
sequence: In summer, the ducks breed on lakes in the cold north.
As winter comes, the lakes freeze and food runs out.
The ducks fly thousands of kilometres to the warm wetlands of Bangladesh.
They spend the winter feeding on the haors and beels.
In spring, they fly back north to breed again.
questions.explanation: Ducks migrate to find food and warmth when their northern homes freeze, then return in spring to breed where there is plenty of food and space.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: A key sorts a hilsa fish, a kingfisher, a cobra and a cow. The first question is 'Does it have legs?'. Yes: kingfisher and cow. No: hilsa and cobra. Which question best separates the kingfisher from the cow?
options: Does it have a backbone?
Does it have feathers?
Does it live in Bangladesh?
Is it an animal?
questions.explanation: A good key question has a clear yes or no and splits the group. Both animals have a backbone, live here and are animals, but only the kingfisher has feathers.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: The Ganges river dolphin is almost blind and uses echoes to find its food. Why is this a useful adaptation in a Bangladeshi river?
questions.model_answer: The river water is muddy, so the dolphin cannot see well. Using echoes (sound) lets it find fish in the muddy water.
questions.explanation: Sight is not much use in muddy water, so the dolphin 'sees' with sound. Its feature matches its habitat, which is what an adaptation is.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Which feature do **all** vertebrates have?
options: wings
six legs
a backbone
a hard skeleton on the outside
questions.explanation: Vertebrates are the animals with a backbone. Wings and six legs belong to insects and some other animals, and an outside skeleton (exoskeleton) belongs to invertebrates.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: The variety of living things in a place is called ___.
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of living things. Bangladesh has high biodiversity, from tigers in the Sundarbans to dolphins in the rivers.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Look at each picture. Sort the animals by where they live.
questions.explanation: Eagles and bats spend much of their life flying, monkeys live in trees, dolphins and crabs live in water, and earthworms live under the ground.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Which numbered part of the skeleton protects the heart and lungs?
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with bones numbered 1 to 6: skull, ribs, spine, pelvis, thigh bone and arm bones.
questions.explanation: Number 2 is the ribs, a cage of bones around the heart and lungs. Number 1 is the skull, which protects the brain.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: The arm in the picture is bending at the elbow joint (4). What are the biceps (2) and the triceps (3) doing?
questions.image_alt: An arm showing the bone, the biceps (contracts), the triceps (relaxes) and the elbow joint, numbered.
options: Both muscles push the bone upwards.
The biceps relaxes and the triceps pushes the bone.
The biceps contracts and pulls the bone, while the triceps relaxes.
Neither muscle moves; the bone bends by itself.
questions.explanation: Muscles can only pull. To bend the arm the biceps contracts (pulls) and the triceps relaxes. To straighten it, the triceps pulls instead.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Match each picture to its vertebrate group.
questions.explanation: Frogs are amphibians, owls are birds, snakes are reptiles, tigers are mammals and goldfish are fish. All five groups have a backbone.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Which of these animals is an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: A crab has no backbone. It has a hard exoskeleton on the outside instead. The tiger, owl and frog all have a backbone.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Insects have six legs. Look at the pictures. Which animals are insects? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Ants and butterflies are insects with six legs. A spider has eight legs, a crab has ten and a worm has none. All five are invertebrates.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: In July Tuli sees no ducks on the haor near her village in Sunamganj. In January the haor is full of ducks that were not there before. What is the best explanation?
options: The ducks hatch from fish in the haor in winter.
The ducks migrate from the cold north to the warm wetlands.
The ducks change into other birds when it gets cooler.
The ducks are fossorial and come up out of the mud.
questions.explanation: Every winter ducks and waders fly thousands of kilometres from cold lands like Siberia to the haors and beels of Bangladesh to find food and warmth.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: A long drought dries up a beel near Rajshahi. A week later the herons that fed on its fish have gone. What is the most likely reason?
options: They flew to a wetland that still has water and food.
They grew gills to live in the mud.
They went underground to wait for the rain.
They turned into fish.
questions.explanation: Natural changes like droughts can change a habitat. Some animals move away to find food and water, while others die.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: A strong cyclone floods and damages part of the Sundarbans. Which things may happen to the animals there? Choose all that are right.
options: Some animals move away to a new place.
Some animals die.
Every kind of animal becomes extinct everywhere the next day.
Some animals find new homes and survive.
The animals' bodies change shape in one night.
questions.explanation: A changed habitat makes some animals move, some die and others find new homes. If a habitat changes too fast a kind of animal may disappear from an area, but animals do not change shape overnight.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Class 4B has finished a minibeast hunt in the school garden. What should they do with the small animals they found?
options: Keep them in a closed box in the sun to study later.
Take them home and keep them for a month.
Handle them gently, keep them shady and put them back where they were found.
Leave them on the hot path so they can dry.
questions.explanation: Minibeasts are living things. Handle them gently, keep them cool and damp, and return them to the place where you found them.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Joy visits Tanguar Haor in winter and sees thousands of migrating birds. Which choices help to protect the birds? Choose all that are right.
options: staying far away from the birds
keeping quiet
taking his litter home
chasing the birds to take photos
joining a boat that goes right into the flock
questions.explanation: Too many people and boats disturb the birds. Staying back, being quiet and taking litter home protect the wetland. Chasing or crowding birds frightens them.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: In the simulation, with the wolves switched on, which bunnies are more likely to survive?

sim.task: Open Natural Selection. Add a mate for the first bunny and choose an environment. Switch on the wolves, then add a fur-colour mutation. Let the bunnies reproduce for a few generations and watch which bunnies the wolves catch.

options: bunnies whose fur colour matches the ground
bunnies whose fur colour stands out from the ground
bunnies that stay in the middle of the field
all bunnies, because wolves catch them equally
questions.explanation: Bunnies with fur that matches their surroundings are camouflaged, so wolves find them less easily. This is an adaptation that helps them survive.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: After many generations with wolves in the simulation, the fur colour that matches the ground becomes more common in the bunny population.

sim.task: Open Natural Selection. Choose an environment and switch on the wolves. Add a fur-colour mutation, let the bunnies reproduce for many generations, and look at the population graph.

questions.explanation: Bunnies that match the ground survive and have babies more often, so their fur colour becomes more common in each new generation.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Example bird counts at a wetland, in thousands: 2019: 50, 2020: 45, 2021: 60, 2022: 38, 2023: 52. Between which two years did the count fall the most?
questions.explanation: The count fell 5 thousand from 2019 to 2020 and 22 thousand from 2021 to 2022. It rose in the other two periods.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Using the same example counts (50, 45, 60, 38 and 52 thousand birds), the mean number of birds counted each year is ___ thousand.
questions.explanation: Add the counts: 50 + 45 + 60 + 38 + 52 = 245. Then divide by the 5 years: 245 ÷ 5 = 49 thousand.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: Class 4B searched for 10 minutes in each place (example data). Under damp leaves they found 6 earthworms, 10 woodlice, 3 ants and 4 snails. On a sunny path they found 1 earthworm and 12 ants. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Ants prefer damp, shady places.
More animals and more kinds lived under the damp leaves than on the sunny path.
Woodlice live in both places.
Sunny paths are the best home for most minibeasts.
questions.explanation: Under the leaves there were 4 kinds and 23 animals, but on the path only 2 kinds and 13 animals. Ants were the only group found more on the path, and no woodlice were found there.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: You are making a key to sort a hilsa fish, a kingfisher, a cobra and a cow. Which would be good questions to use? Choose all that are right.
options: Does it have feathers?
Does it have fins?
Do you like it?
Is it pretty?
Does it have legs?
questions.explanation: Key questions must be about features we can see, with a clear yes or no answer. 'Do you like it?' and 'Is it pretty?' are opinions, so different people would answer differently.

questions.title: Animals of Bangladesh: Diversity and Classification
questions.stem: A new road is built through a forest. Explain how this could change the biodiversity of the forest.
questions.model_answer: The road destroys or cuts up the animals' habitat, so they lose food and shelter. Some animals move away or die, so fewer kinds of animals live in the forest.
questions.explanation: A changed habitat can make animals move away or die. If habitats are lost, fewer kinds of animals can live there, so biodiversity goes down.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Sort these living things into flowering plants, non-flowering plants and things that are not plants.
questions.explanation: Flowering plants make flowers and seeds. Ferns and mosses make spores and pine trees make seeds in cones. Mushrooms and moulds are fungi, not plants.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Match each plant to its adaptation.
pairs: breathing roots that stick up out of salty mud
thick stem that stores water, and spines instead of leaves
waxy leaves that water rolls off
bendy trunk that does not snap in storms
questions.explanation: Each adaptation suits the plant's habitat: air roots for muddy ground, floats for water, a water store for deserts, waxy leaves for wet places and a bendy trunk for storms.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Rice plants do not have flowers.
questions.explanation: Rice is a flowering plant. Its flowers are small and green, so we often do not notice them. The grains of rice are its seeds.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Ferns and mosses do not grow from seeds. They grow from tiny ___.
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses are non-flowering plants. They make tiny cells called spores that can grow into new plants.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: A pine tree makes its seeds inside cones, not flowers. What kind of plant is it?
options: a flowering plant
a fungus
a non-flowering plant
an animal
questions.explanation: Pine trees are conifers, which are non-flowering plants. They still make seeds, but inside cones.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Mushrooms are not plants. They belong to a different group called…
options: fungi
mosses
ferns
conifers
questions.explanation: Mushrooms and moulds are fungi. They cannot make their own food from sunlight, which plants can.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Why do many mangrove trees have roots that poke up out of the mud?
options: to catch fish for the tree to eat
to drink salty water from above
to hold up the flowers
to take in air, because the wet salty mud has very little air
questions.explanation: Roots need air too. The salty mud of the Sundarbans has very little air, so breathing roots grow up into the air.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Tisha says, 'A cactus would grow well in the Sundarbans.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. A cactus is adapted to dry places. In the wet, salty, muddy Sundarbans its roots would rot and it could not survive.
questions.explanation: Adaptations only help in the right habitat. A cactus stores water for dry places, but the Sundarbans is wet and salty, so it would not survive there.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Put these steps in order to show how a storm can harm a rice field near the coast.
sequence: A strong cyclone pushes sea water over the land.
Salty water floods a rice field.
The salt stops the rice roots from taking in water.
The rice grows badly or dies.
questions.explanation: Rice is not adapted to salt. Salty water pushed inland by a storm surge can kill crops, so natural changes can change which plants can grow in a place.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Water hyacinth floats because its leaf stalks are swollen and full of ___.
questions.explanation: The spongy, air-filled stalks work like floats, so the plant stays on the surface while its roots hang down to take in minerals from the water.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which are adaptations of mangrove trees? Choose all that are right.
options: breathing roots that take in air
prop roots that hold the tree steady in soft mud
leaves that can get rid of extra salt
a thick stem that stores water
spongy stalks that make the plant float
questions.explanation: Mangroves live in salty, soft, airless mud. A thick water-storing stem belongs to a cactus and floating stalks belong to water hyacinth.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Water hyacinth is a problem and a gift. Sort these effects.
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth covers ponds and canals, which causes problems. But farmers and craft workers have found clever uses for it, such as floating gardens (dhap) and woven baskets.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: The lotus has long, hollow stems. What is their job?
options: to store water for dry weather
to carry air down to its roots in the mud
to make the plant sink
to hold up the roots like props
questions.explanation: The roots of a lotus are buried in muddy water with little air. The hollow stems carry air down to them.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Look at the mangrove tree. Which labelled part holds the tree steady in the soft mud?
questions.image_alt: A mangrove tree with breathing roots and prop roots in salty mud, labelled breathing roots, prop roots, salty mud and salty water.
options: prop roots
salty mud
breathing roots
salty water
questions.explanation: Prop roots spread out like legs and hold the tree firmly in the soft mud, so storms and tides do not knock it over. The breathing roots take in air.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which of these is **not** a plant?
questions.explanation: A mushroom is a fungus. It cannot make its own food from sunlight, so it is not a plant.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Match each plant to the adaptation that helps it survive.
pairs: waxy leaves that water rolls off
questions.explanation: Water slides off a lotus leaf, a cactus keeps a store of water in its stem for dry weather, and a palm bends in the wind instead of snapping.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which of these are flowering plants? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Sunflowers, lotuses and roses all grow flowers that make seeds. A mushroom is a fungus, so it is not a plant at all.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Where is each plant adapted to live? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: A cactus stores water for deserts, lotus and rice grow in water or flooded fields, and palm trees bend in the strong winds of the coast.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which plant has waxy leaves that water rolls off and long hollow stems that carry air down to its roots in the mud?
questions.explanation: The lotus lives in muddy pools. Its waxy leaves shed water and its hollow stems bring air to the roots.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: A cyclone floods a farm near Khulna with salty sea water. The farmer wants to grow a crop that has a chance of surviving next season. What is the sensible choice?
options: the same ordinary rice, but with more salty water
a cactus, because it stores water
lotus, because it likes standing water
a variety of rice that can grow in slightly salty soil
questions.explanation: Salt-tolerant rice is bred to cope with salty soil. Ordinary rice is not adapted to salt, and a cactus is adapted to dry places, not salty ones.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Mina finds green moss on a damp, shady garden wall. Where else would she be most likely to find moss?
options: on a damp, shady tree trunk
on a hot, dry, sunny road
on a tin roof in the sun
in dry sand
questions.explanation: Mosses are non-flowering plants that grow in damp, shady places, where their spores can grow and they do not dry out.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: A village pond is covered by water hyacinth and the fishing boats are stuck. What is a sensible way to use the plants once they are pulled out?
options: pour strong chemicals into the pond
put them back in the pond to rot
pile them up for compost or a floating vegetable garden
burn them on the pond bank all week
questions.explanation: In Bangladesh people use water hyacinth for compost, cattle food, craft baskets and floating gardens (dhap). Chemicals would harm the fish and the water.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Raju sees green fuzzy mould growing on old bread. He says it is a small plant because it is green and it grows.
questions.explanation: Mould is a fungus, not a plant. It cannot make its own food from sunlight, so it gets its food by growing on the bread.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: People in villages behind the Sundarbans say the forest protects them when a cyclone comes. Why?
options: The mangroves turn the cyclone away from the coast.
The mangroves stop the tide from coming in.
The mangroves make the rain stop.
The mangroves slow the wind and the waves.
questions.explanation: The trees and thick roots of the mangroves slow down the wind and the waves, so less force reaches the villages behind them.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: A patch of water hyacinth covers 3 square metres of a pond and doubles its area every 2 weeks. How much will it cover after 6 weeks?
options: 9 square metres
24 square metres
18 square metres
12 square metres
questions.explanation: After 2 weeks: 6 m². After 4 weeks: 12 m². After 6 weeks: 24 m². 'Doubles' means multiply by 2 each time, not add 3.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Class 4B repeated the model-leaf test (example data). Plain leaves lost 10 g and 14 g of water. Waxy leaves lost 2 g and 4 g. On average, the plain leaves lost ___ times as much water as the waxy leaves.
questions.explanation: Mean for plain leaves = (10 + 14) ÷ 2 = 12 g. Mean for waxy leaves = (2 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3 g. 12 ÷ 3 = 4 times. A waxy coat stops a leaf losing so much water.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Class 4A tests whether a waxy coat stops model leaves (wet paper towels) drying out. Which choices would make the test **unfair**? Choose all that are right.
options: using a bigger paper towel for the waxy leaf
leaving the plain leaves in the shade and the waxy leaves in the sun
using the same amount of water on every leaf
weighing each leaf at the start and again after 3 hours
leaving the waxy leaves for 6 hours and the plain leaves for 3 hours
questions.explanation: Only the wax should change. Different sizes, different places and different times are extra changes. The same water and weighing at the start and end are good practice.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: In a long drought, plant X has small waxy leaves and deep roots. Plant Y has large thin leaves and shallow roots. Which statement is best?
options: X survives better, because waxy leaves make water for the plant.
Y survives better, because large leaves can collect more rain.
Y survives better, because shallow roots are closer to the sun.
X survives better, because waxy leaves lose less water and deep roots reach water underground.
questions.explanation: Small waxy leaves lose little water to the air, and deep roots reach water below the dry surface. Plants do not make water, and large thin leaves lose more of it.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: Joy says, 'Water hyacinth is only a problem. We should destroy all of it.' Give one reason why she may be right and one reason why she may be wrong.
questions.model_answer: She may be right because water hyacinth blocks boats, shades the water so fish get less light and air, and lets mosquitoes breed. She may be wrong because people use it for compost, floating gardens, cattle food and baskets.
questions.explanation: A good answer weighs both sides with evidence. Water hyacinth causes problems for boats, fish and health, but it is also a useful material for farmers and craft workers.

questions.title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation
questions.stem: About a quarter of the Sundarbans was badly damaged by Cyclone Sidr in 2007, but the mangroves grew back over the following years. Hamid says, 'This proves that no kind of plant ever dies out after a cyclone.' Is Hamid's conclusion supported?
questions.explanation: The evidence only shows that the mangroves grew back. It does not tell us about every plant, and natural changes can make some plants die and new kinds take their place.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Put the stages of a frog's life cycle in the right order.
sequence: a tadpole with a tail and gills
a froglet with a short tail
questions.explanation: A frog starts as an egg, hatches into a tadpole, grows legs, becomes a froglet and finally an adult frog that can live on land.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: A seed ___ into a seedling, and a chick ___ from an egg.
questions.explanation: When a seed starts to grow we say it germinates. A chick comes out of its egg when it hatches.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Match each young animal or plant to what it grows into.
questions.explanation: A tadpole grows into a frog, a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, a chick grows into a hen and a seedling grows into an adult plant.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Which features are inherited from parents? Sort them.
questions.explanation: Features such as eye colour and fur colour are passed from parents to young. Scars, haircuts and languages are not inherited: they come from what happens to you or what you learn.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: What do we call the small differences between living things of the same kind, such as kittens of different colours?
options: variation
germination
metamorphosis
migration
questions.explanation: Variation means differences between living things of the same kind. Young are like their parents but never exactly the same.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Tanvir says, 'If I build big muscles at the gym, my children will be born with big muscles.' Is he right?
questions.explanation: Features you gain during your life, like big muscles or a scar, are not inherited. Only features carried from your parents, like eye colour, are passed on.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: What do plants need to grow well? Choose all that are right.
options: light
water
air
minerals from the soil
meat
plastic
questions.explanation: Plants need light, water, air, warmth and minerals from the soil. They make their own food, so they do not need meat.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Compare the life cycles of a chicken and a frog. Which statements are right? Choose all that are right.
options: Both start life as an egg.
A chick changes its body shape a lot, like a tadpole does.
A tadpole breathes with gills and later grows lungs.
A chick looks like a small adult when it hatches.
A frog's young stage lives on dry land.
questions.explanation: Both hatch from eggs. A tadpole lives in water and changes shape (metamorphosis), but a chick already looks like a small hen.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Why does a butterfly lay its eggs on a leaf and not on a stone?
questions.model_answer: When the caterpillar hatches it needs leaves to eat, so the eggs are laid on a plant where it has food straight away.
questions.explanation: A caterpillar hatches hungry and eats leaves all the time. Laying eggs on the right plant gives the young caterpillars food from the start.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Sort these young animals by how they look compared with the adult.
categories: Looks very different from the adult
items: Looks very different from the adult
Looks very different from the adult
Looks very different from the adult
questions.explanation: A tadpole, a caterpillar and a silkworm change their body shape completely as they grow. This is metamorphosis. Chicks, kittens and calves just grow bigger.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: What does a seed need to germinate?
options: light only
soil only
water and warmth
wind
questions.explanation: A seed needs water and the right temperature to start to grow. Light is needed later, once the seedling has leaves.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: A big change of body shape as an animal grows up is called ___.
questions.explanation: Frogs and butterflies go through metamorphosis. Their young look very different from the adults.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: A chicken goes through metamorphosis, like a butterfly does.
questions.explanation: A chick looks like a small version of the adult hen. Butterflies and frogs change their body shape completely, but chickens do not.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Look at the frog's life cycle. Which stage comes straight after the tadpole?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a frog: eggs (frogspawn), tadpole, froglet, adult frog.
options: eggs (frogspawn)
adult frog
chrysalis
froglet
questions.explanation: The tadpole grows legs and loses its tail to become a froglet, and then an adult frog.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Look at the butterfly's life cycle. What happens to the caterpillar inside the chrysalis (pupa)?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a butterfly: eggs, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult butterfly.
options: It lays more eggs.
Its body changes completely into an adult butterfly.
It sleeps and wakes up as a bigger caterpillar.
It turns into a tadpole.
questions.explanation: The chrysalis is a resting stage. Inside it, the caterpillar's body changes completely until an adult butterfly comes out.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Look at the chicken's life cycle. Which statement is right?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a chicken: egg, hatching, chick, adult hen.
options: A chick has a tail and gills like a tadpole.
A chick goes into a chrysalis.
A chick looks like a small hen when it hatches.
A hen turns back into an egg.
questions.explanation: A chicken's life cycle has no big change of shape. The chick hatches looking like a small adult and just grows bigger.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Which numbered stage shows the seed starting to grow into a seedling (germination)?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a flowering plant with seven stages numbered 1 to 7.
questions.explanation: Stage 2 is germination. Stage 1 is the seed, stage 5 is pollination and stage 7 is seed dispersal.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Use the picture of the flowering plant's life cycle. Put the stages in order, starting with the seed.
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a flowering plant with stages numbered: seed, germination, young plant, flowering, pollination, fertilisation and fruit, seed dispersal.
questions.explanation: A seed germinates into a young plant that flowers. Pollen is carried between flowers (pollination), seeds form in a fruit and the seeds are scattered, ready to grow into new plants.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Match each young stage to the adult it grows into.
questions.explanation: A caterpillar changes into a butterfly, a baby chick grows into a hen and a seedling grows into a plant that makes flowers.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Arif grew cress seedlings in a dark cupboard. They grew tall, but they were pale yellow and thin. What should he do to help them become healthy plants?
options: Give them less water.
Keep them in the dark so they grow taller.
Put them in the fridge.
Move them to a light place.
questions.explanation: Plants need light to make food and stay green and strong. Seedlings in the dark stretch tall and thin, looking for light, but they are not healthy.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: A cat in Dhaka has five kittens: two black, two striped and one white. What does this show?
options: The kittens are not from the same mother.
Young animals are like their parents but not exactly the same as each other.
The kittens' fur colour changed because of what they ate.
Only the black kittens are real cats.
questions.explanation: Young inherit features from their parents, but there is always variation. Kittens in one litter can have different colours and patterns.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: The silk for a Rajshahi sari comes from the silkworm, which is the caterpillar (larva) of a moth.
questions.explanation: Silkworms eat mulberry leaves, then spin a cocoon of silk thread around themselves. Inside it becomes a pupa and later an adult moth.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: A silk farmer's silkworms make 12 000 cocoons. One sari needs 3000 cocoons. How many saris can be made?

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Tuli has a cough. Her cousin Rafi offers her some of the medicine his doctor gave him. What should Tuli do?
options: Say no, and tell a trusted adult or a doctor about her cough.
Take the same amount as Rafi.
Take a small amount, just in case.
Mix it with her juice.
questions.explanation: Medicine is a drug that changes how the body works. It is only safe if it is given to you by a doctor or trusted adult for you, in the right amount. Never share it.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: In the simulation, with the wolves on, the fur colour that blends in with the ground becomes more common over many generations. Why?

sim.task: Open Natural Selection. Add a mate for the first bunny and choose an environment. Switch on the wolves, add a fur-colour mutation, and let the bunnies reproduce for many generations. Watch the population graph and the colours of the bunnies.

options: Baby bunnies choose their own fur colour.
Bunnies change their fur colour when they see a wolf.
The wolves change the bunnies' fur colour.
Bunnies with that fur survive longer and pass the colour on to their babies.
questions.explanation: Bunnies whose fur blends in are caught less often, so they have more babies. Babies inherit the fur colour from their parents, so that colour becomes more common.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: In the simulation, a single bunny can change its own fur colour during its life to hide from the wolves.

sim.task: Open Natural Selection. Choose an environment, switch on the wolves and add a fur-colour mutation. Let the bunnies reproduce and watch whether any one bunny changes colour.

questions.explanation: A bunny keeps the fur colour it was born with. The population changes over generations because bunnies that blend in survive and pass their colour on.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Class 4C grew cress for 7 days (example data). Pot A had water, light and warmth: 6 cm. Pot B had no water: 0 cm. Pot C was in the dark: 7 cm, yellow and thin. Pot D was in a fridge: 1 cm. Pot C was the tallest. Does this mean cress grows best in the dark?
options: Yes, because the tallest seedlings are always the best.
Yes, because plants do not need light.
No, because the Pot C seedlings were yellow and thin, so not healthy.
No, because Pot C had no water.
questions.explanation: Height is not the only sign of growth. Seedlings without light grow tall and thin but stay yellow, and they cannot make food. Pot C did have water.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Mina wants to find out whether cress seeds need light to germinate. Which plan is the fairest test?
options: Put 10 seeds in a pot in the light and 20 seeds in a pot in the dark, and water both pots the same.
Use two pots with 10 seeds each, the same soil, water and warmth. Put one in the light and one in the dark. Count the seeds that germinate.
Put one pot in the light and water it every day, and put the other pot in the dark and never water it.
Put 10 seeds in each of two pots. Put one pot in the sun and the other in a dark fridge.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only the light changes. The other plans change more than one thing: the number of seeds, the water or the temperature.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: Many frogs in Bangladesh are disappearing because ponds and wetlands are being filled in for building. Use the frog life cycle to explain why losing ponds is a problem for frogs.
questions.model_answer: Frogs lay their eggs in water, and tadpoles live in water and breathe with gills. Without ponds the eggs and tadpoles cannot survive, so no new frogs can grow up.
questions.explanation: The early stages of a frog's life cycle, the eggs and tadpoles, need water. If the ponds are filled in, the life cycle is broken and the frog population falls.

questions.title: Life Cycles, Growth and Inheritance
questions.stem: A silkworm grows about 10 000 times heavier during its month of eating mulberry leaves. Suppose (example) a newly hatched silkworm has a mass of 1 mg. Its mass after a month is about ___ g. (1 g = 1000 mg)

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Sort the parts of a pond ecosystem into living and non-living.
questions.explanation: Plants, animals, fungi and microbes are living (biotic). Sunlight, water, air, soil, rocks and temperature are non-living (abiotic).

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Put these levels of life in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
questions.explanation: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs and one whole living thing is an organism. Living things of one kind form a population, populations form a community, and a community plus its non-living surroundings is an ecosystem.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Match each example to the type of interaction.
pairs: two trees grow towards the same patch of light
a bee carries pollen while it drinks nectar
a crab hides between mangrove roots
questions.explanation: Living things interact to get what they need. Herons feed on frogs, trees compete for light, bees and flowers help each other, and crabs use roots for shelter.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: All the living things of one kind in a place are a ___, and all the populations living together are a ___.
questions.explanation: All the hilsa in a river are one population. All the different populations (fish, plants, birds, insects) living together make up the community.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Which of these is a **non-living** part of an ecosystem?
options: frog
rock
grass
mushroom
questions.explanation: A rock does not grow, feed, breathe or have young, so it is non-living. A frog, grass and a mushroom are all living things.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: An ecosystem includes only the animals that live in a place.
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is all the living things (plants, animals, fungi, microbes) and the non-living things (sunlight, water, air, soil) in a place, and how they affect each other.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: A rotting log in a garden can be an ecosystem.
questions.explanation: An ecosystem can be big or small. A log has living things (fungi, insects, worms) and non-living things (wood, water), and they all affect each other.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Which are signs that something is living? Choose all that are right.
options: it grows
it feeds
it is green
it senses things around it
it is small
questions.explanation: Living things move, grow, feed, breathe, get rid of waste, sense their surroundings and have young. Being green or small does not make something living.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Two plants grow side by side in a field. What are they most likely competing for?
options: salt and sand
nests and shelter
meat and fish
light and water
questions.explanation: Plants need light and water to make food, and there may not be enough for both. That is why neighbouring plants compete.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Rafi found a dry seed. It does not move or grow. Is it living or non-living? Explain.
questions.model_answer: It is living, but resting. If it gets water and warmth it will germinate and grow.
questions.explanation: A seed is a living thing in a resting state. When it gets water and warmth it germinates and grows, so it is not like a stone.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Why are earthworms helpful to plants?
options: They mix the soil, which helps roots to grow.
They give off light that the leaves can use.
They keep rain from reaching the roots.
They eat the plant's roots to help it grow.
questions.explanation: Earthworms mix the soil and let air and water get in, which makes the soil better for roots. This is an interaction between a living thing and a non-living thing.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Match each living thing and its non-living partner to what happens.
pairs: plants and sunlight, water and air
the plants make their own food
the fish take in dissolved oxygen
shade keeps the ground cooler and damper
the soil is mixed and better for roots
questions.explanation: Living things depend on the non-living parts of their ecosystem for food, air, water and shelter, and they also change those parts.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: A group of parts that work together, so that a change in one part changes the others, is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A pond is a system: its water, plants, fish, birds and sunlight work together. If one part changes, the others change too.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: All the hilsa fish living in the Meghna river are a…
options: community
biosphere
population
organ system
questions.explanation: All the living things of one kind in a place form a population. A community is all the different populations together.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Which numbered part of the pond makes its own food using sunlight, water and air?
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with parts numbered 1 to 8: Sun, air and clouds, duck, fish, water, rock, water plants and frog.
questions.explanation: Number 7 is the water plants. Plants make their own food. The duck (3), fish (4) and frog (8) are animals, so they must eat.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Look at the numbered pond. Sort the numbers into living and non-living parts.
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with parts numbered 1 to 8: 1 Sun, 2 air and clouds, 3 duck, 4 fish, 5 water, 6 rock, 7 water plants, 8 frog.
questions.explanation: The Sun (1), air (2), water (5) and rock (6) are non-living. The duck (3), fish (4), water plants (7) and frog (8) are living.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: The fish (4) take in oxygen that is dissolved in one of the other parts. Which numbered part is it?
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with parts numbered 1 to 8: Sun, air and clouds, duck, fish, water, rock, water plants and frog.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is the water. Fish have gills that take in the oxygen dissolved in the water.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Which numbered part gives the water plants (7) the light they need to make food?
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with parts numbered 1 to 8: Sun, air and clouds, duck, fish, water, rock, water plants and frog.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the Sun. Plants use the light from the Sun, with water and air, to make their food.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Which of these are living things? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Fish are animals, mushrooms are fungi and lotus is a plant, so all three are living. A rock, the Sun and water are non-living.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Match each picture to the interaction.
pairs: gets nectar from flowers and carries pollen
birds nest in trees for shelter
questions.explanation: Bees and flowers help each other, a tree gives a bird shelter for its eggs, and a cow feeds on grass.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: A factory pours hot water into a village pond. The water gets much warmer and holds less oxygen. What is most likely to happen?
options: The fish grow bigger, as warm water has more oxygen.
The fish stay just the same, as water is not alive.
Some fish die or swim away, as there is less oxygen.
The kingfishers get more food, as the water is cleaner.
questions.explanation: Fish take in the oxygen dissolved in water. With less oxygen some fish die or leave, and then the kingfishers that eat them have less food too.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Nadia notices that the soil under a big mango tree is cooler and damper than the soil in the open field. Why?
options: The tree's roots make the soil cold and wet.
The tree gives shade, so the Sun warms the ground less.
The soil under trees is a different kind of rock.
The tree takes all the air out of the soil.
questions.explanation: Trees give shade, which keeps the ground cooler and damper. This is a living thing changing a non-living part of the ecosystem.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Many farmers in Bangladesh keep small fish in their rice fields. Why does this help the farmer?
options: The fish dig up the soil to plant the rice seeds.
The fish stop the rice plants from needing any water.
The fish keep the field warm so the rice grows faster.
The fish eat pests and weeds, and their droppings feed the rice.
questions.explanation: The fish eat insects and weeds, so less pesticide is needed, and their droppings act as fertiliser. The rice gives the fish shade and shelter. They help each other.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: In a long drought a village pond dries up. Which things are likely to happen? Choose all that are right.
options: The fish die.
The kingfishers fly away to find food.
The frogs cannot lay their eggs there.
The water plants grow bigger.
The pond becomes a bigger ecosystem.
questions.explanation: A pond is a system, so a change in one part changes the others. Without water the fish die, the kingfishers lose their food and the frogs lose a place to lay eggs.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Jashim says, 'If all the mangroves in the Sundarbans are cut down, only the trees will be affected.' Is he right?
questions.explanation: Crabs, fish, birds and many other animals use mangroves for shelter and food. In an ecosystem everything is connected, so cutting the trees affects the animals too.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Class 4D put 10 snails in the middle of a tray (example data). After 10 minutes there were 6 snails on the damp side and 2 on the dry side. How many snails were still in the middle?
questions.explanation: 6 + 2 = 8 snails had moved to one side. 10 − 8 = 2 snails were still in the middle.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Class 4D counted snails on each side of a tray every 5 minutes (example data). Damp side: 0, 3, 6, 8, 9. Dry side: 0, 2, 2, 1, 1. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: More snails chose the damp side, so snails seem to prefer damp places.
Every snail prefers damp places, as all moved to the damp side.
The dry side was too hot, so the snails left the tray.
Snails cannot choose where they go, so the results are luck.
questions.explanation: The number on the damp side kept rising to 9 out of 10, while the dry side had only 1. One snail stayed on the dry side, so we cannot say every snail prefers damp. Soft-bodied snails dry out easily.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Example data: a rice-only farm harvested 500 kg of rice and used 6 litres of pesticide. A rice-and-fish farm harvested 520 kg of rice and 60 kg of fish, and used 2 litres of pesticide. A farmer says this proves that fish make rice grow better. What is the best reply?
options: Yes, because 520 kg is more than 500 kg, so fish always help rice.
Yes, because the rice-and-fish farm used a lot less pesticide.
Only two farms were compared, so we need more farms to be sure.
No, because fish cannot affect rice plants in any way at all.
questions.explanation: Two farms may differ in soil, weather or care. We need many farms and repeats before drawing a firm conclusion. The data do show less pesticide (4 litres less) and extra fish.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Heavy rain washes lots of mud into a pond. The water turns cloudy and little light reaches the water plants. What could happen? Choose all that are right.
options: The water plants make less food and may die.
Animals that eat the water plants have less food.
Animals that eat those animals may also go hungry.
The cloudy water makes the Sun shine brighter.
Nothing changes, as mud is non-living.
questions.explanation: Without light the plants cannot make food. The effect passes along: the plant-eaters, and then the animals that eat them, have less food. The parts of an ecosystem are connected.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interactions
questions.stem: Scientists say, 'You cannot change just one thing in an ecosystem.' Explain what they mean, using an example.
questions.model_answer: Everything in an ecosystem is connected, so changing one part affects the others. For example, if trees are removed, the animals lose food and shelter, and the soil gets more sun.
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is a system. Its parts depend on each other for food, shelter, light and water, so a change in one part passes on to the others.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Put these living things in order to make a food chain, starting with the producer.
questions.explanation: A food chain starts with a plant (the producer). Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it: rice plant → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Sort these animals into herbivores, carnivores and omnivores.
questions.explanation: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores eat only animals, and omnivores eat both plants and animals.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Plants are called ___ because they make their own food using energy from the ___.
questions.explanation: Plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air, so they are producers. The energy in every food chain comes first from the Sun.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: In a food chain, the arrow points from the animal to the food that it eats.
questions.explanation: The arrow means 'is eaten by' or 'gives energy to'. It points from the food to the animal that eats it, for example grass → goat.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: What does every food chain start with?
options: a predator
a herbivore
a carnivore
a producer
questions.explanation: Every food chain starts with a producer, a plant that makes its own food using sunlight.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: In the food chain grass → goat → tiger, which living thing is the prey?
options: grass
tiger
goat
the Sun
questions.explanation: Prey is an animal that is hunted and eaten. The tiger is the predator, and the goat is its prey.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: a plant that makes its own food using sunlight
an animal that eats other living things
an animal that hunts other animals
an animal that is hunted and eaten
questions.explanation: Producers make food, consumers eat it, predators hunt, and prey is what they hunt.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Which of these are consumers? Choose all that are right.
options: grass
frog
rice plant
kingfisher
deer
green algae
questions.explanation: Consumers are animals, which cannot make their own food. Grass, rice plants and green algae are plants, so they are producers.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: A frog eats grasshoppers, and a snake eats the frog. What does this show about the frog?
options: It is a producer because it lives near plants.
It is both a predator and a prey animal.
It is a herbivore because it eats insects.
It is only prey because snakes eat it.
questions.explanation: An animal can be both. The frog is a predator of grasshoppers and prey for the snake.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Why do almost all food chains begin with a green plant?
questions.model_answer: Green plants are producers: they make their own food using energy from sunlight. Animals cannot do this, so they get their energy by eating plants or by eating animals that ate plants.
questions.explanation: Only plants (and algae) can capture the Sun's energy to make food. Every other living thing in the chain depends on them for energy.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Where does the energy in a food chain come from first?
options: the Sun
the water
the grass
the soil
questions.explanation: Plants capture energy from sunlight to make food. The grass gets its energy from the Sun, and animals get it from the plants.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: When many food chains in a habitat are joined together, we get a food ___.
questions.explanation: Most animals eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one predator, so the chains join up into a food web.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: A monkey is an omnivore because it eats both plants and animals.
questions.explanation: Omnivores eat both plants and animals. Monkeys, crows and people are omnivores.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Look at the rice-field food chain. Which living thing is the producer?
questions.image_alt: A food chain: grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake.
options: grasshopper
frog
grass
snake
questions.explanation: Grass is a plant, so it makes its own food using sunlight. The grasshopper, frog and snake are consumers.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: In this food chain, which animal is both a predator and prey?
questions.image_alt: A food chain: grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake.
options: grass
frog
snake
grasshopper
questions.explanation: The frog hunts grasshoppers (predator) and is eaten by the snake (prey). The snake is at the end of this chain, and grass is a plant.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Look at the arrow from the deer to the tiger. What does it mean?
questions.image_alt: A Sundarbans food chain: leaves, then deer, then tiger.
options: The tiger eats the deer and gets energy from it.
The deer eats the tiger and gets energy from its body.
The deer gives energy to the leaves.
The tiger is the prey of the deer.
questions.explanation: The arrow points from the food to the eater, so it means 'is eaten by' or 'gives energy to'. The tiger is the predator and the deer is its prey.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Use the pictures to build a rice-field food chain. Put it in order, starting with the producer.
questions.explanation: Rats eat rice, snakes eat rats and eagles eat snakes. The producer (the rice plant) comes first, and the arrows point towards the eater.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Sort the animals by what they eat.
questions.explanation: Cows and deer eat only plants. Tigers and eagles eat only animals. Monkeys and pigs eat both plants and animals.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Match each animal to its food.
questions.explanation: A cow eats grass, a frog eats insects, a tiger hunts deer and a honeybee drinks nectar. Each of these links is one step in a food chain.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Farmers spray a poison that kills most of the frogs in a rice field. What is likely to happen to the grasshoppers?
options: Their numbers go down, because there is less food for them.
Their numbers stay exactly the same in every food web.
They move into the pond to live like frogs.
Their numbers go up, because fewer are eaten.
questions.explanation: Frogs are predators of grasshoppers. With fewer frogs, fewer grasshoppers are eaten, so their numbers may rise and they may eat more of the rice.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Hunters kill too many spotted deer in the Sundarbans. Why could this put villagers in danger?
options: Hungry tigers may come to villages to hunt goats and cows.
The mangrove leaves will stop growing without any deer to eat them.
The tigers will turn into herbivores and eat the village crops.
Angry deer from other forests will move into the villages.
questions.explanation: Deer are the tigers' prey. With fewer deer, tigers have less food and may come closer to villages looking for goats and cows. Protecting the deer protects people and tigers.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Vultures eat dead animals. Across South Asia the number of vultures has fallen a lot. What problem could this cause?
options: Rain falls less often, because there are fewer large birds in the sky.
Cattle grow bigger, because vultures no longer scare them.
Dead animals rot for longer, and disease can spread more easily.
Crops grow better, because fewer birds fly over the fields.
questions.explanation: Vultures are nature's cleaners. Without them dead animals lie for longer, and more stray dogs and rats come to feed on them, so germs spread.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Which actions help to protect a food web? Choose all that are right.
options: giving cattle safe medicines instead of diclofenac
stopping people from hunting too many deer
keeping ponds and wetlands free of poison
spraying poison on all the insects in a field
cutting down all the trees on a river bank
questions.explanation: Diclofenac poisons vultures, hunting too many deer leaves tigers hungry, and poison harms many living things. Protecting the plants and animals in a food web helps all the others.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: The people of a village kill every snake they find near their rice fields. Raju says the number of frogs in the fields might go up.
questions.explanation: Snakes eat frogs. With fewer snakes, fewer frogs are eaten, so the number of frogs may rise. That can then affect the grasshoppers the frogs eat.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Scientists counted living things in a small part of a rice field (example data): 400 rice plants, 60 grasshoppers, 8 frogs and 1 snake. Why are there so few snakes?
options: Snakes cannot live in rice fields because the field is too wet.
Each snake eats many frogs, so only a few can be fed.
Snakes eat rice plants, so they were counted as plants instead.
Frogs eat the snakes, so the snakes are always the smallest group.
questions.explanation: Each animal in a chain needs many of the living things below it to eat. 400 plants feed 60 grasshoppers, which feed 8 frogs, which feed only 1 snake.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: In a rice field (example data) 5 frogs each eat 12 grasshoppers a week. Poison kills 3 of the frogs. Now ___ fewer grasshoppers are eaten each week.
questions.explanation: 3 frogs × 12 grasshoppers = 36. So 36 more grasshoppers survive each week, and they can eat more rice plants.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: In a pond food web, snails and tadpoles eat algae. Fish eat snails and tadpoles. Kingfishers and herons eat the fish. All the fish die. Which things could happen? Choose all that are right.
options: Kingfishers and herons have less food and may leave.
The snails and tadpoles may increase in number.
The algae may decrease, because more snails and tadpoles eat it.
Kingfishers and herons get more food.
Nothing changes, because fish are only one kind of animal.
questions.explanation: Everything in a food web is connected. With no fish, their predators go hungry, their prey increases, and the prey may then eat too much of their own food.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Vultures counted at one site (example data): 200 in 1990, 40 in 2000, 10 in 2010 and 25 in 2020. By what percentage did the count fall from 1990 to 2010?
questions.explanation: The count fell from 200 to 10, a drop of 190. 190 out of 200 is 95 out of every 100, so it fell by 95%. After 2010 the count rose again, perhaps because safer medicines were used.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Explain why protecting the producers is the most important way to protect a whole food web.
questions.model_answer: All the energy in a food web starts with the producers, which make food using sunlight. If the producers die, the herbivores have no food, and then the carnivores have none either, so the whole web is harmed.
questions.explanation: Every other living thing depends on the producers for energy, either directly or by eating something that ate them. If the producers go, the whole web is in trouble.

questions.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
questions.stem: Tuli drew this food chain: tiger → deer → leaves. What is her mistake?
options: The tiger should be placed in the middle of the food chain, not at the start.
Leaves are consumers, so they cannot be part of a food chain.
A food chain must have exactly five living things in it.
The arrows should point from the food to the animal that eats it.
questions.explanation: The arrow shows the way the energy goes, so it points from the food to the eater. Tuli's chain should be leaves → deer → tiger.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Matter is anything that…
options: can be seen and touched
has mass and takes up space
is hot or cold
is always a solid
questions.explanation: Matter has mass and takes up space. This includes things we cannot see, such as air.

questions.title: Matter: States, Elements and Compounds
questions.stem: Air is matter, even though we cannot see it.
